                    ### Question
                    A 65-year-old man is brought into the emergency department by his wife for slurred speech and right-sided weakness. The patient has a significant past medical history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. The wife reports her husband went to bed last night normally but woke up this morning with the symptoms mentioned. Physical examination shows right-sided hemiparesis along with the loss of vibration and proprioception. Cranial nerve examination shows a deviated tongue to the left. What is the most likely diagnosis?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Medial pontine syndrome
opb. Lateral pontine syndrome
opc. Dejerine syndrome
opd. Wallenberg syndrome
ope. Weber syndrome

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with acute neurological symptoms, including right-sided hemiparesis, loss of vibration and proprioception, and a deviated tongue to the left. These findings suggest a left-sided brain lesion affecting the brainstem. The right-sided hemiparesis indicates a left hemisphere lesion, while the loss of vibration and proprioception points to involvement of the dorsal columns, which are affected in brainstem syndromes. The deviated tongue indicates lower motor neuron involvement, likely affecting cranial nerve XII (hypoglossal nerve) on the left side. Medial pontine syndrome is characterized by contralateral hemiparesis and cranial nerve involvement, aligning with the patient's symptoms. Other options, such as Wallenberg syndrome and Weber syndrome, do not fit the symptom profile as closely. Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is medial pontine syndrome.
